neighbours.label: Names of carbohydrates and other biological polymers (chitin, starch, cellulose, glycogen, glucose) in explanatory biochemistry text
fire: Insect wings and beetle shells are stiffened by chitin, a nitrogen-rich polysaccharide.
The liver stores spare glucose as glycogen and releases it between meals.
Wood is mostly cellulose and lignin, which give the trunk its strength.
Potatoes are rich in starch, a long chain of glucose molecules.
Fungal cell walls contain chitin rather than the cellulose found in plants.
Enzymes in saliva begin to split starch into maltose and other simple sugars.
Cows rely on gut microbes to digest the cellulose in grass.
Athletes eat carbohydrates before a race so that their muscles are full of glycogen.
quiet: Insect wings and beetle shells are studied by engineers who design small drones.
The liver sits under the ribs on the right side of the abdomen.
Granite is mostly quartz and feldspar, which give the rock its hardness.
Potatoes are planted in rows and harvested when the leaves die back.
Castle walls contain narrow slits rather than the wide windows found in manors.
Magnets in the motor begin to spin the rotor as the current rises.
Cows rely on farmers to bring them into the barn in winter.
Athletes stretch before a race so that their muscles are warm and loose.
